meta.move: Strong path to the last position
meta.expect: Moves one position at a time on evidence, ends at the rewrite to put this behind him; debrief Where she ended says fair outcome; What she never said names the laptop and how close the 11:31 PM times came

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Hale. I have a client call at 4:40, so let's not waste the time. Who decided to put a zero on Owen's essay, and did anyone speak to him first?
Before anything else: I entered the zero before I called you. That broke procedure 4.2, and I'm sorry Owen found out on his phone.
Okay. Procedure 4.3 says software alone doesn't establish a concern, so what else do you have, Hale?
Here's the version history. Created Wednesday, October 28, 11:31 PM, title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words in one edit. At 11:58 PM, 794 more. No earlier drafts. Turn the screen, read it yourself.
A version history shows when words appeared, Hale, not who wrote them. Procedure 4.1 says you speak with Owen first, so did you, before the zero?
If he drafted somewhere else, he can bring me that file with its dates, and I'll look at it with you.
I'm writing that down. You didn't answer my question about whether you spoke to Owen before the zero. If a file is what you need, the zero comes off while that's sorted.
Second: the essay quotes a line from Act 3, Scene 2 that is not in the play. Here's the act. Search it.
A misquote is a mistake, Hale, and students make them every year. Which line, word for word, and where in the essay is it?
Third: his in-class writing from September 24. 380 words in 40 minutes, comma splices, no quotations. The essay has nine quotations cited by act, scene and line, and no errors.
Forty minutes in a classroom and a week with the play open are not the same conditions, Hale. You still haven't read me the line from Act 3 that you say isn't in the play.

Under 4.4 this is a first concern. I'm offering a supervised rewrite, private, not in front of his class. If it shows the learning, its mark replaces the zero and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.
Okay. That's 4.4, so I'll agree to the rewrite to put this behind him. I want it in an email tonight, copied to the principal: private, nothing on his record, and the zero out of the gradebook now.

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL

Hale,

You agreed to a private, supervised rewrite under 4.4, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing placed on Owen's record. I still want the zero out of the gradebook now and the whole arrangement confirmed in writing, copied to the principal. I expect it in writing tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF

Where she ended: last position, where she agreed to a private supervised rewrite under 4.4, and she still wants the zero out of the gradebook now and your written confirmation copied to the principal; that is the fair outcome, and she got there before her time ran out.
What moved her: you put dated, checkable times in front of her with the version history, then backed it with the September writing sample, so the rewrite offer came after evidence rather than instead of it.
What cost ground: you left the line from Act 3 unread after she asked for it twice, which gave her a gap to call a simple misquote.
What she never said: in October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history, with its late-night times the night before the due date, came very close to that night, but it proves nothing about the essay, and it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: when she asked which line from Act 3 was not in the play, read it aloud word for word and show where it sits in the essay before moving on to the writing sample.
